title: Friends of one another
hook: believing men and women are protectors of one another (9:71)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the cave of Thawr and the quiet helpers around it, and your line was small, brave, ordinary things in the dark. Who did you thank for helping you through something hard? Day four hundred twenty-three.
screen: `SMALL, BRAVE, ORDINARY THINGS IN THE DARK.`

segments.voice: Start with grammar. An Arabic plural like "the believers" can cover a mixed group, the way "you all" does. But in some places the Qur'an says it twice: men and women, believing men and believing women. At-Tawbah does it in verse seventy-one, right after a passage about the hypocrites, men and women, who egg each other on toward wrong. Then the surah turns and describes the other kind of community, and gives it a word: awliya'. Friends. Allies. People who stand at each other's side.

Pickthall translates the verse's opening this way: "And the believers, men and women, are protecting friends one of another; they enjoin the right and forbid the wrong". Then it goes on: they keep up the prayer, they pay the zakat, they obey God and His messenger, and God will have mercy on them. Awliya' is the plural of wali. Its root, w-l-y, carries the sense of being near, next to, close enough to turn toward. So a wali is a friend, but also an ally, a guardian, someone who has your back. The same word can describe God's closeness to believers, and in another verse, a guardian in a family. Here it runs sideways, between people. And look at who is in the list. Men and women share every verb: both encourage good, both push back on wrong, both pray, both give. The verse doesn't divide the work and hand half to each. Why name both at all? A report in Ahmad's Musnad gives one answer. Umm Salama, a wife of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, asked him: why are men mentioned in the Qur'an, and we are not? Later, she heard him reciting from the pulpit a new verse, in Surah al-Ahzab. It names ten qualities, and gives every one of them twice: Muslim men and Muslim women, believing men and believing women, truthful men and truthful women, patient men and women, men and women who give, who fast, who remember God much. For all of them, forgiveness and a great reward. A woman asked a question, and the answer came back spelled out ten times over. Scholars disagree about many details of how men and women work together. This verse is a common starting point: protectors of each other.
screen: `MEN AND WOMEN, PROTECTING FRIENDS.` · `W-L-Y — NEAR, AT YOUR SIDE.` · `THE SAME VERBS FOR BOTH.` · `UMM SALAMA ASKS; TEN PAIRS COME.` · then, large: `PROTECTORS OF EACH OTHER.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath settle. Think of someone of the other sex in your life: a sister, a brother, a colleague, a classmate, a neighbor. Is there a place where their good idea went unheard, or their work got credited to someone else? Picture yourself doing what the verse describes: standing at their side, speaking up for the right thing, simply and decently. If you pray, you can ask for that person by name. The bell holds the time.
Awliya'. Friends, allies, protectors, from a root that means to be near. Believing men and women, at each other's side. Today's word.
Your line: protectors of each other. Today, in one meeting, chat or conversation, make sure one person's good point gets heard and credited to them. Day four hundred twenty-three.

howItsDone: Muslims cite 9:71 when speaking of shared responsibility between men and women in faith and community life; how that cooperation is arranged in mosques, schools and families varies between scholars and communities.

fork.setup: you're Umm Salama. you ask the Prophet why the Qur'an mentions men and not women. what happens next, in the report?
options: he says women are included in the word for men.
a verse comes naming men and women, ten times over.

fork.reveal: later she heard him recite 33:35 from the pulpit, naming every quality twice: for men and for women.

original.note: Arabic: friends, allies, protectors; plural of wali, from the root w-l-y, to be near.

trapdoor: what you thought: friends of one another, a nice sentiment.
what it means: believing men and women are each other's allies and protectors, with the same duties of good.
what a scholar hears: 9:71 answers 9:67, which pairs hypocrite men and women 'of one another' in wrong; the w-l-y root also gives wali, mawla and wilaya.
